citation: What do South African adolescents want in a sexual health service? (2018). South African Medical Journal 108(8). 15 focus groups, 120 adolescents aged 12-19.

Strauss M, Rhodes B, George G (2015). A qualitative analysis of the barriers and facilitators of HIV counselling and testing perceived by adolescents in South Africa. BMC Health Services Research 15:250. doi:10.1186/s12913-015-0922-0

Nyblade L et al. (2022). Stigma in the health clinic and implications for PrEP access and use by adolescent girls and young women: conflicting perspectives in South Africa. BMC Public Health 22:1916. doi:10.1186/s12889-022-14236-z

claims.text: Privacy is the binding constraint: fear of being judged, gossiped about, or exposed by clinic staff makes a service unsafe, so a service is only worth using if it guarantees confidentiality, non-judgmental staff, and separation from adult or HIV-specific areas.
evaluative_rules: Judge a service by whether it protects you from being seen, named, or talked about, not by what it offers on paper
objections: Will anyone find out I came here, and will the staff talk about me?

readings.text: Someone who fears being judged by rude nurses would weigh a new service mainly by whether it keeps them away from staff who might lecture or gossip about them.
If a service separates young people from adult or HIV-specific areas, someone who avoids clinics because of that separation would be more willing to consider it.

Someone who has changed their story or avoided testing because results were shared with teachers or neighbours would only weigh a service seriously if it guaranteed that no one in their community or school would find out.
If a service relies on staff who are known in the community, someone who already moved clinics to avoid neighbours would weigh it as unsafe no matter what else it offers.

claims.text: A positive result is read as a death sentence, so testing is only acceptable when counselling, peer or group support, and messages that HIV is manageable come with it.
evaluative_rules: Judge a testing offer by the support and counselling attached to it, not by the test itself
objections: If the result is positive, will I be counselled and shown how to live with it, or left to fall apart?

readings.text: If a new service offers counselling before testing, someone who believes a positive result is a death sentence would weigh it as a way to avoid doing something wrong after learning their result.
If a new service includes counsellors who say a positive result does not mean the end of your life, someone who feared testing would weigh it as a reason to decide to test.
If a new service provides group testing, someone who gained strength from other guys going to test would weigh it as better than testing alone.
If a new service does not include counselling before testing, someone who thinks counselling helps you know how to take care of yourself would weigh it as a problem.

claims.text: Staff who act like harsh, scolding parents shut down honest disclosure, so a service is only accessible when delivered by younger, relatable, non-parental staff who listen without judging.
evaluative_rules: Judge a service by whether the staff feel like peers who listen, not parents who scold
objections: Will the person I talk to treat me like a child and judge me, or listen and understand?

readings.text: Someone who has been scolded by nurses for being too young would weigh a new service by whether its staff can listen without judging, since harshness holds them back from seeking help.
If a service is delivered by younger staff who are understanding, someone who feels shy with older nurses would weigh it as more accessible because they can become free and not feel shy.
Someone who has seen staff treat adolescents as their own children would weigh a new service by whether staff avoid acting like mothers, because being treated as a daughter makes them close up.

If a service relies on staff who counsel until a teenager changes her mind, someone who wants to be heard without being judged would weigh it as less open, because that staff still acts like a parent.

claims.text: Incomplete or one-size-fits-all information leaves adolescents unable to make informed decisions, so a service is only valuable if it gives complete, accurate, age-appropriate information and individualised choices.
evaluative_rules: Judge a service by whether it gives you full, accurate information and real options, not a single standard answer
objections: Will I be told everything accurately and given choices that fit me, or just handed a standard response?

readings.text: Someone who wants individualised contraception options instead of a one-size-fits-all approach would weigh a new service by whether it presents all available options and lets them choose rather than assigning a standard plan.

If a person has received information that was not age-appropriate and sometimes inaccurate from clinic staff, they would be cautious about a new service until it shows its information is complete and accurate for their age.

Someone who values staff who listen, connect with common adolescent issues, and give relevant practical advice would judge a new service by whether its staff or design make them feel heard and offer ways around barriers.

If a person wants to talk openly and ask questions without fear of being stigmatised or judged, they would weigh a new service by whether it creates a trusting space where they can speak openly to people who relate to them.

region: Five sites in four provinces; Tshwane; rural and peri-urban KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa
confidence: Three qualitative South African studies of young people on sexual health services: 120 adolescents aged 12-19 in 15 focus groups at five sites, 158 learners in KwaZulu-Natal, and young women aged 18-24 in Tshwane. Young people's own accounts only; clinic staff views left out. Mechanisms durable; magnitudes unknown.
subject: being seen, judged or gossiped about when seeking sexual health care
year_note: Three studies: KZN focus groups 2012-2013, Tshwane 2018-2020, five-site adolescent focus groups published 2018.
